title: Cycles of Life: From Pollination to People
subject: Science
description: Comprehensive practice on life cycles: flower parts and pollination, seeds, dormancy and germination, seed dispersal, non-flowering plants, butterfly metamorphosis, bird and human life cycles, and how all cycles connect.

questions.question: According to the book, what is a life cycle?
options: The series of changes a living thing goes through until it produces new life
The number of years a living thing is expected to stay alive in the wild
The change of weather that makes the same flowers bloom every monsoon
The path a seed follows as it is carried away from its parent plant
questions.explanation: The book defines a life cycle as the series of changes a living thing goes through from the beginning of its life to the point where it produces new life, and then the cycle repeats.

questions.question: Which four things do ALL life cycles share, according to the book?
options: Egg, larva, pupa and adult butterfly
questions.explanation: Even though a butterfly, a human and a fern have very different life cycles, all share the same basic pattern: birth, growth, reproduction and death. The other lists are butterfly stages, germination needs and flower parts.

questions.question: The book compares a life cycle to which shape, because it has no real beginning or end?
questions.explanation: A life cycle is 'like a circle, it has no real beginning and no real end' — it keeps coming back to the start.

questions.question: A life cycle has a clear beginning and a clear end, just like a straight line.
questions.explanation: False. The book says a life cycle is like a circle with no real beginning and no real end — it repeats generation after generation.

questions.question: A butterfly's life cycle, a human's life cycle and a fern's life cycle all look exactly the same.
questions.explanation: False. The book says not all life cycles look the same — a butterfly's is very different from a human's, and a fern's is different again. Only the basic pattern (birth, growth, reproduction, death) is shared.

questions.question: All life cycles share the same basic pattern: birth, growth, reproduction and death.
questions.explanation: True. This four-part pattern is the one thing every life cycle in the book has in common, whether it belongs to a plant, an insect or a person.

questions.question: What makes a life cycle different from a straight-line change like ice melting into water?
options: It happens much faster than melting
It only happens to non-living things
It cannot be observed by anyone
It loops back to a new beginning
questions.explanation: The book's review asks this exact question. Ice melting is a one-way change, but a life cycle loops back: the new life it produces starts the whole cycle again.

questions.question: Which example from the book shows a life cycle?
options: A tiny puppy growing into a big dog
Ice melting into water on a hot day
A ball rolling down a sloping road
A cloud drifting across the sky
questions.explanation: The book opens with examples of life cycles you have already noticed: a puppy growing into a dog, a green mango ripening, and the same flowers blooming every monsoon. Melting ice is a straight-line change, not a life cycle.

questions.question: Why does the book say that the same flowers blooming in the same garden every monsoon is NOT a coincidence?
options: Flowers remember the season from the previous year
It is a life cycle repeating generation after generation
The gardener plants the very same seeds each year
Monsoon rain carries pollen in from far-away gardens
questions.explanation: The book says these are not coincidences — they are life cycles, 'nature's way of making sure living things continue to exist, generation after generation.'

questions.question: Select ALL the examples the book uses as signs of a life cycle.
options: A green mango slowly turning yellow and sweet
A tiny puppy growing into a big dog
A stone getting warm in the afternoon sunlight
A kite climbing higher in the wind
questions.explanation: The ripening mango and the growing puppy are the book's own examples of life cycles. A warming stone and a flying kite are not living things, so they have no life cycle.

questions.question: Which statement about a life cycle is NOT true?
options: It repeats itself generation after generation
It can look different in a butterfly and a human
It ends for good when one living thing dies
It has the same basic pattern in all living things
questions.explanation: A life cycle does not end for good — the living thing produces new life before it dies, so the cycle repeats. The other three statements all come straight from the book.

questions.question: Nature uses life cycles to make sure living things continue to exist, generation after generation.
questions.explanation: True. The book calls life cycles 'nature's way of making sure living things continue to exist, generation after generation.'

questions.question: Which word does the book use for the stage when a living thing makes new life?
questions.explanation: Reproduction is the stage when a living thing produces new life. Germination is a seed sprouting, incubation is keeping eggs warm, and dispersal is seeds moving away from the parent.

questions.question: According to the book, a life cycle repeats only in plants, not in animals.
questions.explanation: False. The book follows life cycles through plants, butterflies, birds and humans — every living thing's cycle repeats with each new generation.

questions.question: The book says the cycle returns to the start 'not as a repeat, but as a ___'.
questions.explanation: Each turn of the life-cycle wheel brings new life, so the book calls it a renewal — a fresh start — rather than an exact repeat.

questions.question: Which ride does the book compare life cycles to, because it keeps turning again and again?
questions.explanation: The book says: 'Remember the giant wheel? It keeps turning, again and again. Life cycles work the same way.' Every seed, egg and child is another turn of the wheel.

questions.question: Which part of a flower is colourful and attracts pollinators?
questions.explanation: Petals are 'the attractors' — colourful and often scented, their job is to attract bees, butterflies and other pollinators.

questions.question: What is the job of the sepals?
options: Catch pollen on a sticky tip
Protect the bud before it opens
questions.explanation: Sepals are 'the protectors': small green leaf-like parts that cover and protect the flower bud before it opens, then fold back when the flower blooms.

questions.question: Which part is the MALE part of the flower?
questions.explanation: The stamen is the male part. Its top part, the anther, makes pollen. The pistil is the female part.

questions.question: Which part is the FEMALE part of the flower?
questions.explanation: The pistil is the female part. It has a sticky stigma that catches pollen and leads down to the ovary where seeds form.

questions.question: What does the anther produce?
questions.explanation: The anther is the top part of the stamen and it makes tiny yellow grains called pollen. Seeds form in the ovary, and spores belong to ferns and mosses, not flowers.

questions.question: Which sticky part of the flower catches pollen?
questions.explanation: The stigma is the sticky top of the pistil. Pollen that lands on it travels down to the ovary.

questions.question: In which part of the flower do seeds form?
questions.explanation: The stigma leads down to the ovary, 'where seeds form'. Every fruit you eat began as a flower's ovary.

questions.question: The anther is the top part of which flower part?
questions.explanation: The stamen (male part) has a top part called the anther, which makes pollen.

questions.question: How does the book describe sepals?
options: Pale and white, in the centre
Yellow and powdery, on a stalk
Small and green, below the petals
Bright and red, above the petals
questions.explanation: Sepals are 'small green leaf-like parts below the petals'. The yellow powdery part on a stalk is the anther of the stamen.

questions.question: The stigma is the part of the stamen that produces pollen.
questions.explanation: False. Pollen is produced by the anther, which is part of the stamen. The stigma belongs to the pistil and its job is to catch pollen, not make it.

questions.question: Sepals fold back when the flower blooms.
questions.explanation: True. Sepals cover the bud before it opens and then fold back when the flower blooms.

questions.question: Pollen grains are tiny yellow grains made by the anther.
questions.explanation: True. The book says the anther 'makes tiny yellow grains called pollen', and pollen is needed to help the plant make seeds.

questions.question: A flower's petals are colourful and scented mainly to please people who smell them.
questions.explanation: False. The book says it may seem that way, but 'that is not the case' — bright colours, sweet smell and nectar are there to attract pollinators such as bees and butterflies.

questions.question: In the Try-it investigation, the 'tall stalk with something powdery and yellow on top' is which part?
questions.explanation: The powdery yellow material is pollen, which is made by the anther on top of the stamen. Rubbing your finger on it leaves yellow pollen on your skin.

questions.question: In the Try-it investigation, the 'small green part that was hugging the flower before it opened' is which part?
questions.explanation: Sepals are the small green parts that cover and protect the flower bud before it opens — exactly what the investigation describes.

questions.question: When you pull a flower apart one layer at a time from the OUTSIDE, in which order would you meet the parts?
questions.explanation: Sepals are the outermost protectors below the petals, then come the colourful petals, then the stamens, and finally the pistil, the part 'in the very centre that looks different from the rest'.

questions.question: A flower that blooms at night to attract moths is most likely to have which petals?
options: Dark green petals with sweet nectar
Tiny yellow petals with sticky pollen
Pale petals with a strong fragrance
Bright red petals with a faint scent
questions.explanation: Moths fly at night when colour is hard to see, so night-blooming flowers 'use pale petals and strong fragrance to attract moths'.

questions.question: Select ALL the parts that belong to the pistil (female part).
questions.explanation: The pistil has a sticky stigma leading down to the ovary. The anther is part of the stamen (male part) and petals are the attractors.

questions.question: Select ALL the true statements about the stamen.
options: It is the male part of the flower
It has a sticky stigma at the top
It is where the seeds form
questions.explanation: The stamen is the male part and its anther makes pollen. The sticky stigma and the ovary where seeds form both belong to the pistil.

questions.question: Which flower does the book suggest using for the pull-it-apart investigation?
questions.explanation: The investigation says: 'What you need: One real flower like Hibiscus, a magnifying glass, and a paper plate.'

questions.question: What happens when you rub your finger on the yellow powdery top of a stamen?
options: Yellow pollen sticks to your finger
Sweet nectar drips onto your finger
The petal folds back and closes up
A seed drops out of the flower
questions.explanation: The powder is pollen, tiny yellow grains made by the anther. It sticks to your finger just as it sticks to a visiting bee.

questions.question: What is pollination?
options: Change of an animal's shape as it grows up
Transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
Movement of seeds away from the parent plant
Waking of a seed that absorbs water and sprouts
questions.explanation: Pollination is 'the transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of the same or another flower'. The others describe seed dispersal, germination and metamorphosis.

questions.question: What are the three main ways pollen travels?
options: By roots, by leaves, or through the stem
By rain, by rivers, or along the sea
By wind, by animals, or within the same flower
By water, by sunlight, or through the soil
questions.explanation: The book lists three ways: by wind, by animals, or within the same flower. Rivers and the sea carry seeds (dispersal), not pollen.

questions.question: Why do pollinators such as bees and butterflies visit flowers?
questions.explanation: Pollinators visit flowers to drink nectar. As they do, pollen sticks to their bodies and is carried to the next flower.

questions.question: Which description fits a wind-pollinated flower?
options: Small, not brightly coloured, no strong smell
Large, brightly coloured, strong sweet smell
Colourful, full of nectar, sticky pollen
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers are usually small, not brightly coloured, have no strong smell, produce no nectar, and often grow in groups. They do not need to attract anyone.

questions.question: Which of these plants is wind-pollinated?
questions.explanation: Wheat, grass, maize, rice, bamboo and pine are the book's wind-pollinated examples. Mango, apple and rose rely on animals.

questions.question: Which of these plants relies on animals for pollination?
questions.explanation: Rose, mango, sunflower, apple, hibiscus and cotton are animal-pollinated. Bamboo, maize and grass are wind-pollinated.

questions.question: Why do wind-pollinated plants make such LARGE amounts of pollen?
options: So animals have plenty of pollen to eat as their food
So the heavy pollen sinks quickly into the soil below
So the flowers look bright yellow from far away
So at least some drifts to another flower of the same kind
questions.explanation: Wind is not a reliable carrier, so these plants make large amounts of light, dry pollen 'so that at least some of it can drift to another flower of the same species'.

questions.question: What is pollen from a wind-pollinated plant like?
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated plants make light, dry pollen that can drift on the air. Animal-pollinated flowers make sticky pollen that clings to visitors.

questions.question: Why is the pollen of an animal-pollinated flower sticky?
options: So it tastes sweet and attracts more insects
So it clings to the body of a visiting animal
So it drifts easily on the wind to other flowers
So it can sink down into the ovary by itself
questions.explanation: Animal-pollinated flowers have 'sticky pollen that clings to a visitor's body', so the pollen travels with the animal to the next flower.

questions.question: Which feature tells you a flower depends on WIND, not animals, for pollination?
options: Small size and no strong smell
questions.explanation: This is the book's review question. Wind-pollinated flowers are small and have no strong smell; bright petals, nectar and sticky pollen are all signs of animal pollination.

questions.question: A farmer's wheat field needs no bees to produce grain, but his mango orchard next to it does. Why?
options: Wheat has no flowers at all while mango grows large flowers
Mango trees are too tall for the wind to reach their flowers
Wheat makes seeds without pollen while mango needs pollen
Wheat is wind-pollinated while mango relies on animal pollinators
questions.explanation: Wheat is one of the book's wind-pollinated plants, so the wind carries its pollen. Mango is animal-pollinated, so it depends on bees, butterflies or bats to move its pollen.

questions.question: Bats are major pollinators of which fruits in many parts of the world?
questions.explanation: The 'Night pollinators' box says bats are major pollinators of fruits such as bananas and mangoes.

questions.question: What kind of flowers attract bats?
options: Yellow flowers that produce no nectar at all
Pale, night-blooming flowers with strong fruity smells
Bright red day flowers with lots of sticky pollen
Tiny green flowers that grow in large groups
questions.explanation: Bats come out at night, so they are attracted to pale, night-blooming flowers with strong fruity smells that they can find in the dark.

questions.question: A flower opens only at night, has pale petals and a strong fragrance. Which visitors is it most likely trying to attract?
questions.explanation: The book says some flowers bloom at night and 'use pale petals and strong fragrance to attract moths'. Bees and butterflies visit during the day.

questions.question: Why is pollen important for a plant?
options: It is the food the plant stores in its roots
It protects the flower bud before it opens
It carries water from the soil to the petals
It is needed to help the plant make seeds
questions.explanation: The book says plainly: 'Pollen is needed to help the plant make seeds.' Without pollination there are no seeds, fruits or new plants.

questions.question: Every fruit you have ever eaten began as which part of a flower?
questions.explanation: The book says every fruit — mango, tomato, banana, watermelon — began as a flower's ovary, the place where seeds form.

questions.question: According to the book, why does a fruit form around the seeds?
options: To give the flower's petals a bright new colour
To protect the seeds and attract animals to carry them away
To stop pollen from reaching the sticky stigma
To keep the seeds dormant forever inside the plant
questions.explanation: The fruit 'forms to protect the seeds inside, and to attract animals to eat it and carry those seeds far away' — so fruit helps with seed dispersal.

questions.question: Wind-pollinated flowers usually produce lots of sweet nectar.
questions.explanation: False. Wind-pollinated flowers produce NO nectar and have no strong smell — they do not need to attract animals.

questions.question: Pollination can happen within the same flower.
questions.explanation: True. The book lists three ways pollen travels: by wind, by animals, or within the same flower.

questions.question: Bats pollinate flowers mainly during the day.
questions.explanation: False. Bats are night pollinators, attracted to pale, night-blooming flowers with strong fruity smells.

questions.question: Pine is an example of a wind-pollinated plant.
questions.explanation: True. Pine appears in the book's list of wind-pollinated plants, and its male cones release large amounts of pollen carried by the wind.

questions.question: Animal-pollinated flowers often grow in large groups so the wind can reach them easily.
questions.explanation: False. Growing in groups is a feature of WIND-pollinated flowers. Animal-pollinated flowers rely on colour, scent and nectar instead.

questions.question: Select ALL the wind-pollinated plants.
questions.explanation: Rice and bamboo are in the book's wind-pollinated list. Cotton and apple are animal-pollinated.

questions.question: Select ALL the features of an animal-pollinated flower.
questions.explanation: Animal-pollinated flowers have colourful petals, a noticeable scent, nectar and sticky pollen. 'No nectar' and 'grows in groups' describe wind-pollinated flowers.

questions.question: In the paper-flower investigation, what did the cotton ball represent?
options: A seed being dispersed by an animal
A flower's sticky stigma catching pollen
A bee carrying pollen between flowers
The wind blowing pollen off a flower
questions.explanation: You pressed the cotton ball ('bee') into Flower A, pollen stuck to it, and then you moved it to Flower B — so you were acting like a pollinator.

questions.question: In the paper-flower investigation, what did the yellow chalk powder or turmeric stand for?
questions.explanation: The pinch of yellow powder placed in the centre of Flower A was the 'pollen' that the cotton-ball 'bee' carried to Flower B.

questions.question: The book calls pollination 'one of nature's most remarkable ___'.
questions.explanation: Pollination is a partnership: the pollinator gets nectar to drink and the plant gets its pollen carried to another flower.

questions.question: Which is NOT a usual feature of a wind-pollinated flower?
options: Sticky pollen that clings to visitors
Small flowers that are not bright
No strong smell and no nectar
questions.explanation: Sticky pollen belongs to animal-pollinated flowers. Wind-pollinated flowers make light, dry pollen and are small, dull, unscented and grow in groups.

questions.question: When a bee drinks nectar and then flies to another flower, what is the bee actually doing for the plant?
options: Spreading spores so new plants can grow
Keeping the flower warm like a parent bird
Carrying pollen on its body to the next flower
Carrying seeds from the fruit to new ground
questions.explanation: As the bee drinks nectar, pollen sticks to its body and is carried to the next flower it visits — this is pollination.

questions.question: What is dormancy?
options: The stage when a seed sprouts a root
The time a seed spends floating on water
The moment a seed's coat splits open
A resting state, a kind of deep pause
questions.explanation: A seed is 'a living thing in a resting state called dormancy, a kind of deep pause'. It is alive but switched off, waiting for the right conditions.

questions.question: What lies inside a dormant seed?
options: A tiny embryo, a miniature plant switched off
A drop of nectar to feed visiting insects
A pinch of pollen waiting for the wind
A cluster of spores ready to be released
questions.explanation: Inside a seed lies 'a tiny embryo: a fully formed miniature plant, switched off and waiting for the right conditions to begin growing'.

questions.question: Why is dormancy called a survival strategy?
options: Dormant seeds float better and travel further by water
Sprouting too soon on dry or frozen ground could mean death
A dormant seed can make its own food using sunlight
A resting seed is too hard for any animal to eat
questions.explanation: If the seed sprouted at the wrong time — on dry or frozen ground — the young plant would die. So the seed waits, sometimes for years, until conditions are just right.

questions.question: Where did scientists find the 2,000-year-old date palm seed that they grew into a tree?
options: In a cave in the Seychelles
In an ancient jar in Israel
questions.explanation: The book says scientists found a 2,000-year-old date palm seed in an ancient jar in Israel and grew it into a tree.

questions.question: Which is the world's largest seed?
questions.explanation: The world's largest seed is the Coco de mer from the Seychelles. Orchid seeds are the world's smallest.

questions.question: Up to how much can a Coco de mer seed weigh?
questions.explanation: The Coco de mer from the Seychelles can weigh up to 25 kg — heavier than many children!

questions.question: Which plants have the world's smallest seeds?
questions.explanation: Certain orchids have seeds so tiny that a single gram can hold over a million seeds.

questions.question: About how many orchid seeds can fit in a single gram?
questions.explanation: Orchid seeds are so tiny that 'a single gram can hold over a million seeds'.

questions.question: A dry mung bean seed that shows no movement and no growth is dead.
questions.explanation: False. The book says most people would guess it is dead, 'but it isn't'. The seed is alive in a resting state called dormancy.

questions.question: A seed may wait for months or even years before it germinates.
questions.explanation: True. The seed waits, 'sometimes for months or even years, until conditions outside are just right'.

questions.question: The giant Coco de mer seed and a tiny orchid seed are built from completely different parts.
questions.explanation: False. The book says both 'contain the same basic parts, doing the same basic job' — size does not change what a seed is.

questions.question: What do the world's largest seed and the world's smallest seeds have in common?
options: The same weight of about one gram each
Both come from the Seychelles islands
Both need sunlight before they can sprout
The same basic parts doing the same basic job
questions.explanation: Despite the huge size difference, the book says both contain the same basic parts doing the same basic job.

questions.question: Which dried seeds does the book ask you to look at as examples of dormancy?
questions.explanation: The book says: 'Look at a dried mung bean or mustard seed. It's hard, dry, and still' — yet it is alive.

questions.question: Which part of a seed stores the food the embryo needs until its first green leaves appear?
questions.explanation: The book says that until the seedling breaks through the soil, 'the cotyledon's stored food is all it needs'.

questions.question: When you open a soaked bean seed, which THREE things does the book ask you to find?
options: Baby root, baby shoot, food store
questions.explanation: The Try-it says: 'open one soaked seed into two halves. Try to find the baby root, the baby shoot, and the food store.'

questions.question: A seed has been lying dry and still in a cupboard for two years. What is the BEST description of it?
options: Dead, because it has not grown for so long
Already a seedling that stopped growing
Rotten, because seeds live only a few months
Alive but dormant, awaiting right conditions
questions.explanation: Seeds can stay dormant for months or years. The 2,000-year-old date palm seed proves a dry, still seed can still be alive.

questions.question: What is the process called by which a seed reawakens, absorbs water and sprouts into a new seedling?
questions.explanation: Germination is 'the process by which a seed reawakens, absorbs water and sprouts, growing into a new seedling'.

questions.question: Which THREE things does a seed need from its surroundings before it germinates?
questions.explanation: A seed needs three signals that say 'It is safe to grow now': water, warmth and oxygen. Sunlight is NOT on the list.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT needed for a seed to germinate?
questions.explanation: The book asks 'Did you notice what is not on the list?' — sunlight. Most seeds germinate underground where there is little or no light.

questions.question: Why does a germinating seed NOT need sunlight?
options: It makes its own light from the enzymes inside it
Sunlight would dry out the soft seed coat too quickly
The seed coat is too thick for any light to pass through
It germinates underground using the cotyledon's stored food
questions.explanation: Most seeds germinate underground where there is no sunlight; the stored food in the cotyledon is all the seed needs until its first green leaves appear.

questions.question: What does WATER do for a germinating seed?
options: Softens the seed coat and activates enzymes
Keeps the embryo cool and slows reactions
Carries the seed away from the parent plant
Gives the seedling its green colour
questions.explanation: Water 'softens the seed coat and activates the enzymes that begin digesting the stored food. Without water, nothing starts.'

questions.question: What temperature range do most seeds prefer for germination?
questions.explanation: Each species has an ideal range, but the book says most seeds prefer 20–30°C.

questions.question: What happens to a seed if it is TOO HOT?
questions.explanation: The book says: 'Too cold and reactions slow; too hot and the embryo dies.'

questions.question: What happens to a seed if it is TOO COLD?
questions.explanation: Cold does not kill the seed straight away — 'too cold and reactions slow'. Too much heat is what kills the embryo.

questions.question: Why does a germinating seed need OXYGEN?
options: Energy for breaking down food and building cells needs oxygen
Oxygen softens the hard seed coat so the root can push out
Oxygen gives the first leaves their green colour
Oxygen carries the pollen to the stigma of the flower
questions.explanation: The germinating seed is 'working hard, breaking down food, building cells. All of that requires energy, and energy needs oxygen.'

questions.question: When does sunlight become important for a new plant?
options: Only when the plant is ready to make flowers
After the seedling breaks through the soil
Before the seed absorbs any water at all
While the seed is still dormant underground
questions.explanation: Sunlight 'becomes important only after the seedling breaks through the soil and its first green leaves appear'.

questions.question: Until its first green leaves appear, what does a seedling live on?
questions.explanation: Until the seedling reaches the light, 'the cotyledon's stored food is all it needs'.

questions.question: Into how many precise steps does the book divide germination?
questions.explanation: The book calls germination 'a sequence of five precise steps that transform a dormant seed into a seedling pushing towards the sun'.

questions.question: When a new plant begins to grow, which way do the roots and shoots grow?
options: Roots grow downward, shoots grow upward
Roots grow upward, shoots grow downward
Both roots and shoots grow sideways
Both roots and shoots grow downward
questions.explanation: The book says that after germination 'roots grow downward, shoots grow upward, and a new plant begins its life cycle'.

questions.question: Why does a seed remain dormant instead of germinating right away?
options: It cannot absorb any water at all
It waits for safe conditions to sprout
It has no embryo inside it yet
It needs sunlight to become alive
questions.explanation: This is the book's review question. The seed already has an embryo and can absorb water; it waits so it does not sprout on dry or frozen ground where it would die.

questions.question: A seed can germinate underground without sunlight.
questions.explanation: True. Most seeds germinate underground where there is little or no light; sunlight only matters once green leaves appear.

questions.question: A seed needs water, warmth and oxygen to germinate.
questions.explanation: True. These are the three signals that tell a seed it is safe to grow.

questions.question: A seed will still germinate even if one of its three signals is missing.
questions.explanation: False. The book says: 'If even one signal is missing, the seed stays dormant.'

questions.question: Every plant species has exactly the same ideal temperature range for germination.
questions.explanation: False. 'Each species has an ideal temperature range', though most seeds prefer 20–30°C.

questions.question: Select ALL the signals a seed needs before it will germinate.
questions.explanation: Water, warmth and oxygen are the three signals. Sunlight is not needed until the seedling is above the soil, and fertiliser is not on the book's list.

questions.question: Which statement about germination is NOT true?
options: Too much heat kills the embryo
Oxygen is needed to release energy
A seed needs sunlight to sprout
questions.explanation: Sunlight is the one thing NOT on the seed's list of needs. Water, a safe temperature and oxygen are all required.

questions.question: In the bean-seed investigation, how long should you soak the seeds?
questions.explanation: Step 1 of the investigation is 'Soak the bean seeds overnight' before opening one to find the baby root, baby shoot and food store.

questions.question: A gardener keeps a seed warm and gives it plenty of water, but seals it in an airtight jar. What will most likely happen?
options: It stays dormant because it has no oxygen
It germinates faster because it is protected
It sprouts but grows only roots, not shoots
It germinates because water and warmth are enough
questions.explanation: A seed needs all three signals — water, warmth AND oxygen. With no oxygen there is no energy for growth, so the seed stays dormant.

questions.question: What is seed dispersal?
options: Release of spores from the brown dots under a fern leaf
Movement of seeds away from the parent plant to new places
Transfer of pollen from one flower to another flower
Waking of a dormant seed when it absorbs water
questions.explanation: Seed dispersal is 'the movement of seeds away from the parent plant to new locations, where they can germinate and grow without competing with the parent'.

questions.question: Why is it a problem if seeds fall directly below the parent plant?
options: They will be eaten by the parent plant's roots
They get too much shade and turn into spores
They compete with the parent for light, water and space
They cannot germinate without the parent's pollen
questions.explanation: Seeds under the parent 'will have to compete with it for sunlight, water, and space', so nature has ways to spread seeds to new places.

questions.question: A bird eats ripe berries from a bush and flies across a field. Where are the seeds most likely to be left?
options: Back inside the same berry on the bush
Only in the bird's nest high in a tree
Stuck to the bird's feathers and beak
In its droppings, far from the parent bush
questions.explanation: The bird digests the fruit and passes the seeds out in its droppings far away — this is how fruits help seeds travel.

questions.question: Which of these seeds is carried by WATER, according to the answer key?
questions.explanation: Coconut, water lily and lotus seeds float and are carried by rivers, rain, ponds or the sea.

questions.question: How do coconut, water lily and lotus seeds travel to new places?
options: They are eaten by birds and dropped later
They float along rivers, ponds or the sea
They stick to animal fur with tiny hooks
They drift on the wind with fluffy hairs
questions.explanation: The answer key says these seeds 'float and are carried by rivers, rain, ponds or the sea'.

questions.question: Megha finds a seed that is light and fluffy with tiny hair-like strands. How does it most likely travel?
options: By animals, stuck to their fur
By wind, drifting through the air
By water, floating on a river
questions.explanation: Light, fluffy seeds with hair-like strands are built to catch the wind and drift far from the parent plant.

questions.question: Megha's other seed is hard, heavy and covered in tiny hooks that stick to her sock. How does it most likely travel?
options: By floating down a stream to the sea
By drifting on the wind like a feather
By bursting out of a dry seed pod
questions.explanation: Hooks that stick to a sock would also stick to an animal's fur, so the seed is carried away until it falls off somewhere new.

questions.question: If Megha plants both seeds in the same pot right next to each other, will they both grow well?
options: No — they would compete for light, water and space
Yes — two seeds always help each other grow
Yes — hooked seeds and fluffy seeds never compete
No — seeds can never grow in a small pot
questions.explanation: The whole point of dispersal is to avoid competition. Two plants crowded together must share the same sunlight, water and space, so neither grows as well.

questions.question: How do fruits help seeds travel?
options: Fruits catch pollen from passing insects
Animals eat the fruits and carry the seeds elsewhere
Fruits float on the wind like tiny parachutes
Fruits keep the seeds dormant for many years
questions.explanation: The 'Cycles Connect' page says: 'Animals eat fruits and carry the seeds to new places, helping new plants grow away from the parent plant.'

questions.question: A mango tree produces flowers which become fruits with new seeds. Which stage of the life cycle is the flowering stage?
questions.explanation: The flowering stage belongs to reproduction, because the tree is making new seeds.

questions.question: After a mango tree forms new seeds, how does the life cycle begin again?
options: The tree drops all its leaves and grows new flowers
The seeds turn back into pollen and travel by wind
The fruits reattach to the branch and ripen again
The seeds spread to new places and germinate
questions.explanation: The answer key says: 'The new seeds are spread to new places and germinate into new plants, so the cycle repeats.'

questions.question: A farmer wants many new strawberry plants from one healthy plant. Which method should the farmer use?
options: Dispersal of seeds by the wind
questions.explanation: The answer key says the farmer should use vegetative reproduction through runners, 'because runners grow along the ground and form new plants wherever they take root'.

questions.question: Why do strawberry runners work well for making new plants?
options: They release pollen that the wind carries far away
They grow along the ground and root to form new plants
They float on water and sprout wherever they land
They are carried in bird droppings to new fields
questions.explanation: Runners are stems that grow along the ground; wherever they take root, a new strawberry plant forms — no seeds needed.

questions.question: Seed dispersal means seeds falling directly below the parent plant.
questions.explanation: False. Dispersal is the opposite — seeds moving AWAY from the parent so they do not compete with it.

questions.question: Coconut seeds can float and be carried by water.
questions.explanation: True. Coconut, water lily and lotus seeds float and travel by rivers, ponds or the sea.

questions.question: Seeds that pass through a bird are destroyed and can never grow.
questions.explanation: False. Seeds in bird droppings land far from the parent plant and can germinate there — this is one way fruits help seeds travel.

questions.question: Seed dispersal helps new plants grow away from the parent plant.
questions.explanation: True. This is one of the book's own Checkpoint statements, and it is correct.

questions.question: Select ALL the seeds the answer key says are carried by water.
questions.explanation: Coconut, water lily and lotus are the water-carried examples. Wheat and pine are wind-pollinated plants, not water-dispersed seeds.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a resource the book says seeds must compete for if they stay near the parent?
questions.explanation: The book names sunlight, water and space. Pollen is for making seeds, not something a seedling competes for.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: What do non-flowering plants reproduce WITHOUT?
questions.explanation: Non-flowering plants such as ferns and mosses 'reproduce without flowers or seeds', using spores instead.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: What are the little brown dots under a fern leaf called?
questions.explanation: The little brown dots under a fern leaf are called sori, and they hold spores.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: What do the sori of a fern hold?
questions.explanation: Sori hold spores. When ready, they split open and release the spores into the air.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Where must a fern spore land to grow into a new fern?
questions.explanation: If a spore lands on damp soil, it can grow into a new fern plant.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Mosses are described in the book as some of the ___ plants on Earth.
questions.explanation: The book says mosses are 'some of the oldest plants on Earth'.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Where does a moss keep its spores?
options: In tiny capsules on thin stalks
In brown dots under its leaves
In the scales of a woody cone
In the ovary of a small flower
questions.explanation: Moss spores 'are kept in tiny capsules on thin stalks'. The brown dots under leaves are the sori of ferns.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Why do mosses grow in damp, shadowy places?
options: Because the wind cannot reach there
Because they need water to reproduce
Because their roots are very deep
questions.explanation: The book says 'mosses need water to reproduce, so they grow in damp, shadowy places'.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Which of these trees is a conifer?
questions.explanation: Pine trees, cedars and firs are called conifers. They produce seeds on cones instead of inside fruits.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Which tree has seeds that sit naked on the scales of a cone?
questions.explanation: Conifers like pine have seeds that are not enclosed in fruits — they sit naked on the scales of a cone.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: How is pollen carried from male cones to female cones in a conifer?
questions.explanation: Male cones release large amounts of pollen 'which is carried by the wind to female cones'.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: On which cones do conifer seeds develop after fertilisation?
questions.explanation: After fertilisation, seeds develop on the female cones. When the cones open, the seeds are released.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: When are conifer seeds released?
options: When the cones fall into water
questions.explanation: The book says: 'When the cones open, the seeds are released.' Cones have no petals and do not need bees.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Ferns reproduce using seeds.
questions.explanation: False. This is one of the book's Checkpoint statements and it is false — ferns reproduce using spores held in sori.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Mosses need water to reproduce.
questions.explanation: True. This Checkpoint statement is correct; that is why mosses live in damp, shadowy places.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Conifer seeds are enclosed inside fleshy fruits.
questions.explanation: False. Conifers 'produce seeds, but their seeds are not enclosed inside fruits. Their seeds sit naked on the scales of a cone.'

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Both ferns and mosses use spores to reproduce.
questions.explanation: True. Ferns keep spores in sori under their leaves; mosses keep spores in capsules on thin stalks.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Select ALL the conifers named in the book.
questions.explanation: Pine trees, cedars and firs are the book's conifers. Mango and rose are flowering plants.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Select ALL the plants that reproduce using spores.
questions.explanation: Ferns and mosses use spores. Pine makes seeds on cones; wheat is a flowering plant that makes seeds.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: How is the way a fern reproduces DIFFERENT from the way a mango tree reproduces?
options: The fern needs bees to carry its spores; the mango needs the wind
The fern grows seeds inside cones; the mango grows seeds in sori
The fern needs sunlight to reproduce; the mango needs water
Fern uses spores, no flowers or seeds; mango uses flowers and seeds
questions.explanation: Mango is a flowering plant — pollination and seeds. Ferns are non-flowering and release spores that grow on damp soil.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Which of these is NOT a non-flowering plant?
questions.explanation: Ferns and mosses reproduce by spores and conifers like pine by cones — all without flowers. A sunflower is a flowering, animal-pollinated plant.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Unlike a fern, a conifer DOES make something. What is it?
options: Seeds, but not inside a fruit
questions.explanation: Conifers produce real seeds — but they sit naked on cone scales rather than inside a fruit. Ferns make spores, not seeds.

questions.topic: Non-flowering Plants: Ferns, Mosses and Conifers
questions.question: Fill in the blank from the book's review: 'Ferns and mosses reproduce using ___ instead of seeds.'
questions.explanation: Both ferns and mosses release spores that can grow into new plants if they land in a damp place.

questions.question: The word 'metamorphosis' comes from Greek words meaning 'change' and ___.
questions.explanation: The word comes from Greek words meaning 'change' and 'form' — a change of body form.

questions.question: What is metamorphosis?
options: A process in which an animal's body changes shape as it grows
A process in which a seed reawakens and sprouts into a new seedling
A process in which a baby grows bigger but keeps the same shape
A process in which parent birds keep their eggs warm
questions.explanation: Metamorphosis is 'a biological process in which an animal's body changes shape and structure as it grows', for example from a larva into an adult.

questions.question: Which of these animals does NOT undergo metamorphosis?
questions.explanation: Humans, dogs and elephants are born looking like small versions of the adults and simply grow bigger. Insects (like butterflies and moths) and frogs undergo metamorphosis.

questions.question: Which TWO groups of animals does the book say undergo metamorphosis?
questions.explanation: The book says 'many animals such as insects and frogs undergo metamorphosis'. Humans, dogs and elephants do not.

questions.question: What are the four stages of a butterfly's life cycle in the correct order?
questions.explanation: The four stages are egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis) and adult butterfly.

questions.question: Why does a female butterfly choose one exact plant species for her eggs?
options: That plant will be food for the caterpillars after they hatch
That plant has the sweetest nectar for the adult butterfly
That plant's flowers are pale and bloom only at night
That plant has the strongest stem for the chrysalis to hang
questions.explanation: She picks the plant 'because it will provide food for the caterpillar after they hatch'.

questions.question: How does a female butterfly check that she has found the right plant?
options: She rubs pollen on the leaves
She tastes the leaves with her feet
She smells the flowers with her antennae
She drinks the nectar with her proboscis
questions.explanation: The book says 'she tastes leaves with her feet to make sure it is the right plant'.

questions.question: Why does a female butterfly lay her eggs on the UNDERSIDE of a leaf?
options: To make the eggs easy for birds to find
To help the eggs catch pollen from the wind
To keep the eggs safe from rain and predators
To let sunlight warm the eggs quickly
questions.explanation: The underside of a leaf keeps the eggs 'safe from rain and predators'.

questions.question: What is a caterpillar's ONE main job?
questions.explanation: When the egg hatches, the caterpillar comes out 'with one main job: eat'. It eats almost constantly.

questions.question: Why does a caterpillar shed its skin several times?
options: It grows so fast it needs room for a bigger body
Its old skin turns into the hard chrysalis
Its skin becomes the wings of the adult
Birds cannot see it while it changes skin
questions.explanation: A caterpillar eats almost constantly and grows so fast that 'it sheds its skin several times to make room for a bigger body underneath'.

questions.question: Why does a caterpillar eat almost constantly?
options: To keep the leaf warm for the other eggs
To grow fast and store energy for the big change
To make nectar for the adult butterfly to drink
To grow its wings while it is still a larva
questions.explanation: All this eating 'stores up energy for the big change ahead' — the transformation inside the chrysalis.

questions.question: What is the hard case formed by the caterpillar at the pupa stage called?
questions.explanation: The caterpillar forms a hard case called a chrysalis. From outside it seems still, but major changes happen inside.

questions.question: What actually happens to the caterpillar's body inside the chrysalis?
options: It grows wings directly on its existing body
It simply gets bigger and grows a hard shell
Nothing changes until the shell cracks open
Most breaks down and surviving cells rebuild a new body
questions.explanation: Special chemicals break down most of the caterpillar's body into liquid; clusters of special cells survive and use that material to build wings, antennae and legs.

questions.question: A butterfly has just come out of its chrysalis with soft, folded wings. What happens to its wings soon after?
questions.explanation: The adult emerges with soft, folded wings 'that soon expand and harden' so it can fly.

questions.question: What is the long tube-like mouthpart of an adult butterfly called?
questions.explanation: The adult butterfly drinks nectar 'through a long tube-like mouthpart called a proboscis'.

questions.question: How does the proboscis help an adult butterfly?
options: It helps the butterfly break out of the chrysalis
It carries pollen back to the caterpillar
It lets the butterfly drink nectar from flowers
It lets the butterfly taste leaves for its eggs
questions.explanation: The proboscis is a drinking tube: the adult 'drinks nectar from flowers, instead of chewing leaves like a caterpillar'.

questions.question: What does an adult butterfly do to begin the cycle again?
options: Finds a mate and lays eggs
questions.explanation: After its wings harden, the adult 'finds a mate and lays eggs, beginning the cycle again'.

questions.question: An insect hatches from an egg as a worm-like larva, later forms a hard case, and finally comes out as an adult with wings. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Larva → hard case (pupa) → winged adult is a complete change of body form: metamorphosis.

questions.question: A caterpillar eats leaves all day, while the adult butterfly only drinks nectar. Why do they need such different food?
options: They are really two different animals that happen to look related
The caterpillar grows and stores energy; the adult mainly flies, mates and lays eggs
The caterpillar has a proboscis; the adult has chewing jaws for leaves
The caterpillar needs sugar for its wings; the adult needs leaves for its legs
questions.explanation: The larva's job is eating and growing to store energy for the change; the adult's job is to fly, find a mate and lay eggs, and nectar is the quick fuel for that.

questions.question: From the OUTSIDE, a chrysalis appears still. What does the book say is really happening?
options: The caterpillar is slowly eating the case
Wings are growing on the outside of the case
The caterpillar is resting, nothing changes
questions.explanation: 'From the outside, it appears still, but major changes are happening inside' — the body is being rebuilt.

questions.question: A newly hatched caterpillar looks like a small adult butterfly.
questions.explanation: False. The book says the caterpillar 'doesn't look like the adult butterfly at all' — that is what makes it metamorphosis.

questions.question: The word 'metamorphosis' comes from Greek words.
questions.explanation: True. It comes from Greek words meaning 'change' and 'form'.

questions.question: Frogs undergo metamorphosis.
questions.explanation: True. The book names insects and frogs as animals that undergo metamorphosis.

questions.question: A caterpillar chews leaves, while the adult butterfly drinks nectar.
questions.explanation: True. The adult drinks nectar through its proboscis 'instead of chewing leaves like a caterpillar'.

questions.question: Butterfly eggs are laid on TOP of leaves so that sunlight can warm them.
questions.explanation: False. Eggs are laid on the UNDERSIDE of a leaf, safe from rain and predators.

questions.question: The chrysalis (pupa) is the stage in which the butterfly eats the most.
questions.explanation: False. The larva (caterpillar) is the eating stage. Inside the chrysalis the body is being broken down and rebuilt, not fed.

questions.question: Select ALL the adult body parts built from the broken-down material inside the chrysalis.
questions.explanation: The surviving cells build 'the wings, antennae, and legs of the adult butterfly'. An egg tooth belongs to a bird chick, and the chrysalis itself is the hard case.

questions.question: Select ALL the animals that undergo metamorphosis.
questions.explanation: Butterflies (insects) and frogs change body form as they grow. Elephants and dogs are born as small versions of the adults.

questions.question: A puppy looks like a small dog from the day it is born. What is this kind of growth called?
questions.explanation: Growing bigger without a dramatic change of shape is called direct development.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a butterfly stage with its other name?
questions.explanation: The larva is the caterpillar, and the pupa is the chrysalis.

questions.question: Which stage of the butterfly life cycle is described as 'the changing stage'?
questions.explanation: The book labels the stages: egg (the beginning), larva (the eating stage), pupa (the changing stage) and adult (the flying stage).

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Do birds go through metamorphosis?
options: Yes — but only large birds like eagles
No — because birds never grow after hatching
No — a chick is a small version of its parents
Yes — a chick changes into a completely new form
questions.explanation: 'Birds don't go through metamorphosis. A chick hatches looking like a small version of its parents and gradually grows into an adult.'

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Which THREE special features does the book give for bird life cycles?
options: Soft-shelled egg, no parental care, slow growth
Chrysalis, proboscis and soft folded wings
Spores, tiny capsules and damp soil
Hard-shelled egg, parental care, fast growth
questions.explanation: Bird life cycles have 'a hard-shelled egg, strong parental care, and fast growth'.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: A bird's egg has a hard shell with tiny pores. What passes through these pores?
questions.explanation: The hard shell protects the chick 'but lets air pass through tiny pores'.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: What do the yolk and the egg white give the chick?
options: Both give the chick its feathers
The yolk gives food, the egg white gives water
The yolk gives water, the egg white gives food
The yolk gives air, the egg white gives warmth
questions.explanation: The answer key says: 'The yolk gives food to the chick and the egg white gives it water.'

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: What is incubation?
options: A young bird learning how to fly
A caterpillar forming a hard case
Parents sitting on eggs to keep them warm
A chick breaking out of its shell
questions.explanation: 'Parent birds keep the eggs warm by sitting on them, this process is called incubation.'

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: A chick breaks its shell using a sharp point on its beak called the egg ___.
questions.explanation: When fully developed, the chick breaks the shell using a sharp point on its beak called an egg tooth.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: A chick that has just broken out of its shell is called a ___.
questions.explanation: A hatchling is a chick that has just hatched. A fledgling is older and learning to fly.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: A young bird that is learning to fly is called a ___.
questions.explanation: 'A young bird learning to fly is called a fledgling.'

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Which bird does the book give as an example of a chick that hatches with open eyes, soft feathers, and can walk right away?
questions.explanation: Some chicks hatch blind and featherless, 'others, such as ducks, hatch with open eyes, soft feathers, and can walk right away'.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: What do chicks that hatch blind and featherless need?
questions.explanation: Chicks that hatch blind and featherless need 'full parental care' until they grow feathers and get stronger.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: What do parent birds do during the nestling and fledgling stage?
options: Feed and protect the chick while it learns to hop, find food and fly
Leave the nest so the chick must find its own food at once
Keep sitting on the chick to incubate it for many months
Carry the chick in their beaks to a new nest each day
questions.explanation: 'Parents feed and protect it while it learns to hop, find food, and fly.'

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Why do many adult birds lay their eggs at a time when food is easy to find?
options: So the eggs blend in with ripe fruit nearby
So parents can find food for the chicks easily
So the eggs stay cool in the hot season
So the chicks can fly away sooner
questions.explanation: Egg-laying is 'often timed to when food is easy to find' so parents can feed the hungry chicks.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: What is the correct order of a bird's life cycle?
questions.explanation: The book's diagram shows: 1. Egg, 2. Hatchling, 3. Fledgling, 4. Adult. Egg-larva-pupa-adult is a butterfly's cycle.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: In the Checkpoint ordering task, which event should be numbered 1 (first)?
options: The chick breaks out using its egg tooth
The hatchling grows feathers and learns to fly
The adult finds a mate and builds a nest
Parent birds sit on the eggs to keep them warm
questions.explanation: Incubation comes first, then hatching, then the fledgling stage, and finally the adult breeding to start the next cycle.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Is a bird's life cycle an example of metamorphosis?
options: No — the chick is already shaped like its parents
Yes — the hatchling has no feathers and the adult does
Yes — the egg stage is like a chrysalis
No — because birds do not have a life cycle
questions.explanation: Metamorphosis means a change of body shape and structure. A chick is already shaped like its parents, so birds do NOT undergo metamorphosis.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Why does a mother bird build a nest BEFORE laying her eggs?
options: To hide herself from the hungry fledglings
To keep the eggs safe and warm during incubation
To store food for when the chicks can fly
To attract bees and other pollinators to the tree
questions.explanation: The nest holds the eggs together so the parent can sit on them to keep them warm (incubation) and protect them.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Which is one way the human life cycle is SIMILAR to a bird's life cycle?
options: Both have a stage where they shed their skin to grow
Both drink nectar through a long tube-like mouthpart
Neither goes through metamorphosis; young look like small adults
Both hatch from a hard-shelled egg with tiny pores
questions.explanation: The answer key lists similarities: both go through birth/hatching, growth, reproduction and death; neither undergoes metamorphosis; and the young of both receive care from parents.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: A chick breaks its shell using its egg tooth.
questions.explanation: True. The egg tooth is a sharp point on the chick's beak used to break the shell.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: The egg white gives the chick food, and the yolk gives it water.
questions.explanation: False. It is the other way round: the yolk gives food and the egg white gives water.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: A fledgling is a bird that has just broken out of its shell.
questions.explanation: False. A bird that has just hatched is a hatchling. A fledgling is a young bird learning to fly.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Birds go through metamorphosis just like butterflies.
questions.explanation: False. Chicks hatch looking like small versions of their parents and simply grow — no metamorphosis.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Incubation means a parent bird sits on the eggs to keep them warm.
questions.explanation: True. This warmth lets the chick develop inside the egg.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Select ALL the correct egg-part and job pairs.
questions.explanation: Yolk = food, egg white = water. The shell protects the chick and its pores let AIR through, not nectar or sunlight.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: At which stage does a bird grow feathers and begin learning to fly?
questions.explanation: 'As the chick grows, feathers develop and it becomes stronger' — this is the nestling/fledgling stage, after hatching and before adulthood.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycle: Eggs, Care and Flight
questions.question: Which statement about a bird's egg is NOT true?
options: The shell is sealed so no air can pass
The yolk is the chick's store of food
The egg white provides the chick water
The hard shell protects the chick
questions.explanation: The shell protects the chick but has tiny pores that let air pass through — it is not completely sealed.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Which bird's FATHER keeps the egg warm on his feet during the freezing Antarctic winter?
questions.explanation: The table says the emperor penguin father keeps the egg warm on his feet during the freezing Antarctic winter.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Which bird is one of the longest-living birds on Earth?
questions.explanation: The wandering albatross is 'one of the longest-living birds on Earth'.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Which bird's chicks can walk soon after hatching?
questions.explanation: Chicken chicks take only a few hours to start walking.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Which bird's parents continue feeding the young even after they learn to fly?
questions.explanation: The table says bald eagle parents 'continue feeding young birds even after they learn to fly'.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Which bird's chicks hatch blind and helpless?
questions.explanation: House sparrow chicks hatch blind and helpless, yet grow up in about 2 weeks.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: How long does a house sparrow's egg take to hatch?
questions.explanation: The table gives 11–14 days for the house sparrow — the shortest in the list.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: About how long does a chicken's egg take to hatch?
questions.explanation: A chicken egg takes about 21 days to hatch.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: About how long does an emperor penguin's egg take to hatch?
questions.explanation: An emperor penguin's egg takes about 65 days, kept warm on the father's feet.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: About how long does a bald eagle's egg take to hatch?
questions.explanation: A bald eagle's egg takes about 35 days to hatch.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: About how long does a wandering albatross egg take to hatch?
questions.explanation: The wandering albatross egg takes about 80 days — the longest in the table.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: How long does a house sparrow take to grow up?
questions.explanation: House sparrows grow up in about 2 weeks — very fast compared with penguins or albatrosses.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: How long does an emperor penguin chick take to grow up?
questions.explanation: Emperor penguin chicks take 5–6 months to grow.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: How long does a wandering albatross chick take to grow up?
questions.explanation: A wandering albatross takes about 9 months — the longest growing time in the table.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: How long does a bald eagle chick take to grow up?
questions.explanation: Bald eagle young take 10–12 weeks to grow, and parents keep feeding them even after they fly.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Which bird in the book's table has the egg that takes the LONGEST to hatch?
questions.explanation: Albatross about 80 days > penguin about 65 > eagle about 35 > chicken about 21 > sparrow 11–14.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Which bird in the table has the egg that hatches the FASTEST?
questions.explanation: The house sparrow's 11–14 days is the shortest hatching time in the table.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Chicken chicks can start walking within a few hours of hatching.
questions.explanation: True. The table says chickens take 'a few hours to start walking'.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: The emperor penguin MOTHER keeps the egg warm on her feet through the Antarctic winter.
questions.explanation: False. It is the FATHER who keeps the egg warm on his feet during the freezing Antarctic winter.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Not all baby birds grow in the same way — some hatch helpless while others can walk soon after hatching.
questions.explanation: True. Sparrows hatch blind and helpless, but chickens and ducks can walk almost at once.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Bald eagle young are fully grown in about 2 weeks.
questions.explanation: False. Bald eagles take 10–12 weeks to grow. It is the house sparrow that grows up in about 2 weeks.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Select ALL the birds that take MONTHS (not weeks) to grow up, according to the table.
questions.explanation: Emperor penguins take 5–6 months and albatrosses about 9 months. Sparrows grow up in about 2 weeks and chickens walk within hours.

questions.topic: Bird Life Cycles Can Be Very Different
questions.question: Which statement about the birds in the table is NOT true?
options: The eagle's parents feed it even after it can fly
The chicken's egg takes longer to hatch than the eagle's
The sparrow grows up faster than the penguin
The albatross egg takes longer to hatch than the penguin's
questions.explanation: A chicken egg hatches in about 21 days, an eagle's in about 35 — so the chicken's is shorter, not longer.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Into how many stages do scientists divide human life?
questions.explanation: Scientists divide human life into five stages: infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: What is 'direct development'?
options: Growth in which the body changes shape completely, like a caterpillar
Growth of a seed into a seedling using stored food
Growth of feathers on a chick while it learns to fly
Growth without dramatic change — a baby simply grows bigger
questions.explanation: In humans 'a baby simply grows, slowly and steadily, into an adult who looks similar, just bigger. This is called direct development, growth without dramatic change.'

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: What is the approximate age range of INFANCY?
questions.explanation: Infancy is 0–2 years: the brain doubles, bones harden and the baby learns to see, hear, move and say first words.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: What is the approximate age range of CHILDHOOD?
questions.explanation: Childhood is 2–10 years: steady growth, milk teeth replaced, and learning language, reading, maths and social skills.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: What is the approximate age range of ADOLESCENCE?
questions.explanation: Adolescence is 10–18 years: growth spurt, hormones, body shape changes, identity and independence.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: What is the approximate age range of ADULTHOOD?
questions.explanation: Adulthood is 18–60 years: full size is reached, with gradual slowing after the mid-40s.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: At what age does OLD AGE begin, according to the book's table?
questions.explanation: Old age is listed as 60+ years: slower healing, weaker bones, reduced energy — and a time for experience, teaching and sharing knowledge.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Which body change happens in INFANCY?
options: The brain doubles and bones harden
Milk teeth are replaced by adult teeth
questions.explanation: In infancy the brain doubles, bones harden and there is rapid weight gain. Milk teeth are replaced in childhood; the growth spurt is adolescence; slower healing is old age.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: In which stage are milk teeth replaced?
questions.explanation: Childhood (2–10 years) brings steady growth, replacement of milk teeth and better coordination.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Which stage is marked by a growth spurt, hormones and changes in body shape?
questions.explanation: Adolescence (10–18 years) is the stage of growth spurt, hormones and body-shape changes, with growth in identity, independence and deeper thinking.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Which stage is described as 'reaches full size; gradual slowing after mid-40s'?
questions.explanation: Adulthood (18–60 years) is when the body reaches full size, with gradual slowing after the mid-40s.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: What kinds of growth does the book list for OLD AGE?
options: Language, reading, maths and social skills
Seeing, hearing, moving and first words
questions.explanation: Old age is a time for 'experience, teaching, sharing knowledge, helping others'. The other lists belong to infancy, adolescence and childhood.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: About how many bones is a baby born with?
questions.explanation: Babies are born with about 300 bones, while adults have 206.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: How many bones does an adult have?
questions.explanation: Adults have 206 bones because some of the baby's roughly 300 bones fuse together as we grow.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Why do adults have FEWER bones than babies?
options: Some bones fuse to form stronger bones
Some bones fall out like milk teeth
Some bones shrink and disappear in old age
Babies are counted twice by mistake
questions.explanation: 'As we grow, some bones fuse together to form stronger bones, including the skull.'

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: How does the book describe a baby's skull?
options: Thin plates that fall off and regrow each year
Soft pieces that slowly fuse to protect the brain
One hard bone that never changes shape or size
A hollow shell with tiny pores that let air in
questions.explanation: The skull 'starts as soft pieces and slowly fuse together, to protect the brain'.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Which animal can jump and hide soon after hatching, already knowing how to survive?
questions.explanation: The book contrasts the grasshopper, which can jump and hide soon after hatching, with a human baby who cannot walk, talk or care for itself.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Why do humans have such a long childhood?
options: Our bones take years to harden fully
We have fewer bones than other animals
We must wait for our milk teeth to grow
Our brains take years to develop
questions.explanation: 'Our brains take years to develop, giving us time to learn and understand the world.'

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Why do human babies need many years of care compared with a butterfly caterpillar?
options: Human brains take years to develop survival skills
Humans have weaker bones than caterpillars
Humans do not grow at all after they are born
Caterpillars do not have any parents to help them
questions.explanation: This is the book's review question. Humans must learn speaking, reading, problem-solving and staying safe — skills that take a developing brain many years.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: What pattern does the book notice about animals with larger, more complex brains?
options: More babies, longer to grow up, no parental care
Fewer babies, longer to grow up, much more parental care
More babies, faster growth, less parental care
Fewer babies, faster growth, no parental care
questions.explanation: 'Animals with larger, more complex brains tend to have fewer babies, take longer to grow up, and receive much more parental care.'

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: About how many eggs does the frog in the book lay before walking away?
questions.explanation: 'The frog lays 4,000 eggs and walks away' — the opposite of the elephant, whose whole herd raises one calf.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: How does the elephant care for its young, according to the book?
options: It lays thousands of eggs and leaves them behind
It has one calf and leaves it alone to grow up
It has many calves raised by the father
It has one calf and the whole herd helps raise it
questions.explanation: 'The elephant has one calf and the whole herd helps raise it.'

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Priya is 9. Two milk teeth fell out and new ones grew, and she is much better at reading and sums. Which stage is she in?
questions.explanation: Age 9, milk teeth being replaced, and rapid progress in reading and maths are all signs of childhood (2–10 years).

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Mr. Verma is 65, walks a little slower, and his bones take longer to heal. Which stage is he in?
questions.explanation: Age 65 is 60+, and slower healing and weaker bones are the book's old-age body changes.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Which part of the case shows Mr. Verma living out old age as a time for 'teaching, sharing knowledge, helping others'?
options: His bones taking longer to heal after a fall
Being 65 years old, past the start of old age
Teaching Priya card games and sharing childhood stories
Walking a little slower than he used to in the past
questions.explanation: Teaching card games and sharing stories is exactly the 'experience, teaching, sharing knowledge' kind of growth the book lists for old age.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Humans go through metamorphosis as they grow.
questions.explanation: False. Humans grow by direct development — a baby grows steadily into a similar-looking, bigger adult.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: An adult has more bones than a newborn baby.
questions.explanation: False. A baby has about 300 bones and an adult only 206, because bones fuse together as we grow.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Adolescence is roughly the years from 10 to 18.
questions.explanation: True. The table gives adolescence as 10–18 years.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Milk teeth are replaced during infancy.
questions.explanation: False. Milk teeth are replaced in childhood (2–10 years). Infancy (0–2) is when the brain doubles and bones harden.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Humans have the longest childhood, the most parental care, and the most to learn.
questions.explanation: True. The book says humans are 'at the far end of this pattern'.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Select ALL the body changes of INFANCY.
questions.explanation: Infancy: brain doubles, bones harden, rapid weight gain. Milk-teeth replacement is childhood; the growth spurt is adolescence.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Select ALL the kinds of growth the book lists for OLD AGE.
questions.explanation: Old age brings experience, teaching, sharing knowledge and helping others. First words are infancy; the growth spurt is adolescence.

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Match the description to the stage: 'Rapid brain growth; first words appear; completely dependent on parents.'
questions.explanation: Rapid brain growth and first words are the hallmarks of infancy (0–2 years).

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Match the description to the stage: 'Slower healing; weaker bones; sharing wisdom and experience.'
questions.explanation: Slower healing and weaker bones, together with sharing wisdom, describe old age (60+).

questions.topic: The Human Life Cycle: Five Stages
questions.question: Which statement about human growth is NOT true?
options: A long childhood lets the brain develop
A baby changes shape completely, like a caterpillar
The skull starts as soft pieces that fuse together
Humans can keep learning at every age of life
questions.explanation: Humans grow by direct development, not metamorphosis. The other three statements are all from the book.

questions.topic: What Stays the Same Through Life
questions.question: What does the book call the 'tiny instructions' inside your body?
questions.explanation: 'Inside your body are tiny instructions called DNA.' They help decide features like eye colour and hair type.

questions.topic: What Stays the Same Through Life
questions.question: Which features does DNA help decide, according to the book?
options: Favourite food, best friend and hobbies
Number of teeth, bones and fingers
Reading speed, maths skill and memory
Eye colour, hair type and height pattern
questions.explanation: DNA helps decide features such as eye colour, hair type and height pattern.

questions.topic: What Stays the Same Through Life
questions.question: Does a person's DNA change as they grow older?
options: No — it stays the same throughout life
Yes — it changes at every life stage
Yes — but only after old age begins
